elements.markdown: The trace gives us two concrete targets: repeated per-account queries take **620 ms of the 900 ms server response**, then rendering 2,000 table rows takes **350 ms**. I recommend investigating query batching first and exploring a smaller rendered table alongside it. Those timings identify opportunities, not guaranteed savings: we still need the query plan. SQL and frontend changes are available; adding infrastructure is outside the current authorization. Billing must reflect edits immediately, while summary reporting can tolerate up to 30 seconds of lag.

elements.multi: Which improvements should we explore together?

options.description: Targets the largest measured cost; a query plan must show whether round trips, scans or joins dominate.
Targets the 350 ms browser cost; pagination or virtualization changes navigation and must preserve full-data search.

Batch the account queries.markdown: A set-based query could replace repeated account lookups, but batching can also create a large join or change totals through duplicate rows. I’ll inspect the existing SQL and query plan before choosing a rewrite. Fresh billing reads should remain on the immediate post-edit path; the 30-second allowance applies only to summaries.

Batch the account queries.select: What should the SQL work produce next?

options.description: Inspect the repeated SQL, parameter patterns and execution plan; return a justified rewrite proposal before changing behavior.
Prepare an editable design now, with query-plan validation required before implementation.

Investigate the query plan first.default: Inspect the per-account queries and their execution plans using representative dashboard parameters. Identify repeated round trips, scans, row counts and join fan-out. Compare candidate set-based SQL with the current query results, including billing immediately after an edit. Report the evidence and proposed SQL change before implementation.

Investigate the query plan first.markdown: The next decision depends on that evidence: repeated cheap queries favor batching; expensive scans or join fan-out need a different SQL design. I won’t assume which case we have.

Draft a batching proposal.default: Fetch the required accounts in a set-based query and preserve existing account permissions, totals and ordering. Validate the plan and result equivalence before adopting the rewrite. After a billing edit, refresh the affected billing data immediately; do not apply the summary lag allowance to billing. Use the current infrastructure.

Draft a batching proposal.check: Also investigate whether separating summaries from fresh billing would help

reveals.markdown: Separating these reads may let summaries refresh less often without delaying billing, but we have no evidence of an existing cache or a cheap refresh mechanism. First inspect how summaries are produced and updated within the current system.

reveals.default: Evaluate a separate summary refresh path using existing infrastructure, with at most 30 seconds of lag. Keep billing updates immediately visible and document how refresh failures are detected. Recommend a mechanism only after inspecting the current data flow.

Render fewer table rows.markdown: Reducing mounted rows can reduce rendering work without narrowing the searchable data. Search must run over all 2,000 rows before choosing what to display. Pagination provides explicit page navigation; virtualization keeps scrolling but requires careful focus, keyboard and screen-reader behavior. We have not inspected those interaction requirements yet.

Render fewer table rows.select: Which table approach should we investigate or prototype?

options.description: Identify keyboard navigation, editing, selection and accessibility constraints before selecting a rendering technique.
Limits mounted rows with explicit navigation; users may lose continuous scanning across accounts.
Keeps continuous scrolling with a small mounted window; focus and accessibility need verification.

Inspect table interactions first.default: Inspect how the table implements search, keyboard navigation, focus, screen-reader semantics, inline edits and selection across rows. Identify which interactions require the full table. Recommend pagination, virtualization or another rendering change only after reviewing those constraints.

Prototype pagination.default: Prototype 50 rows per page. Apply search and sorting to the complete data set before pagination; show total matches and explicit page controls. Preserve selection across pages and immediately refresh edited billing values. Measure render time and verify keyboard and screen-reader navigation before adoption.

Prototype virtualization.default: Prototype a visible row window with modest overscan. Apply search and sorting to the complete data set before windowing. Preserve row identity, selection and active edit state; keep focused rows usable when scrolling. Verify keyboard and screen-reader workflows and immediate billing updates before adoption.

elements.markdown: Pursuing both targets should improve different parts of the wait. Benchmark the SQL and table changes separately before measuring them together, so one improvement cannot hide a regression in the other. Search completeness and immediate post-edit billing are acceptance checks for the combined design.
elements.when: selected(improvements, Batch the account queries) && selected(improvements, Render fewer table rows)

elements.input: Joint validation proposal — edit if needed
elements.default: Use the same representative dashboard data to compare the baseline, SQL-only change, table-only change and both together. Measure server query time, response time and browser rendering. Verify full-data search, result equivalence, keyboard navigation and immediately visible billing edits. Stop and revise the proposal if correctness or interaction checks fail.
elements.when: selected(improvements, Batch the account queries) && selected(improvements, Render fewer table rows)
